qs.q: A 29-year-old construction worker is unable to push against a wall with his right arm and demonstrates posterior displacement of the scapula. Which nerve and corresponding muscle are most likely affected?
qs.e: Injury to the long thoracic nerve causes paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle, leading to the clinical sign of a winged scapula. The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor, which abducts and rotates the arm.
qs.s: Anatomy Marathon 1 — Lower Limb — Revision Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A 22-year-old hypertensive patient is found to have delayed lower extremity pulses and prominent, pulsating vessels around the scapula. Which physiological mechanism explains these collateral scapular vessels?
qs.e: In coarctation of the aorta distal to the subclavian artery, blood is diverted through the subclavian branches, markedly enlarging and making the collateral vessels of the scapular anastomosis visibly pulsate. Subscapular bursitis is an inflammatory condition unrelated to aortic coarctation.
qs.s: Anatomy Marathon 1 — Lower Limb — Revision Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A patient presents with 'winging of the scapula' after a radical mastectomy where the chest wall was deeply dissected. Which nerve and corresponding muscle are most likely injured?
o: Long thoracic nerve and serratus anterior
Dorsal scapular nerve and levator scapulae
qs.e: The long thoracic nerve runs over the outer surface of the serratus anterior, and its injury results in winging of the scapula due to paralysis of this muscle. The thoracodorsal nerve supplies the latissimus dorsi instead.
qs.s: SDL Revision Mock Marathon — Upper Limb, Histology & Embryology —: MCQs

qs.q: A patient presents with an inability to lift their arm above the horizontal plane due to impaired upward rotation and protraction of the scapula. Which muscle and nerve are most likely involved?
o: Pectoralis major supplied by the medial pectoral nerve
Trapezius supplied by the spinal accessory nerve
Levator scapulae supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve
Serratus anterior supplied by the long thoracic nerve
qs.e: Serratus anterior protracts and rotates the scapula upward, which is essential for full arm abduction above the horizontal, and is innervated by the long thoracic nerve. Trapezius also assists in scapular movement but is innervated by cranial nerve XI.
qs.s: SDL Revision Mock Marathon — Upper Limb, Histology & Embryology —: MCQs

qs.q: A patient presents with a winged scapula and difficulty elevating the arm above the horizontal. Which nerve is primarily responsible for the motor innervation of the affected muscle?
qs.e: The trapezius muscle is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve. The thoracodorsal nerve instead supplies the latissimus dorsi.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The scapula is a flat, triangular bone that anchors shoulder muscles and provides a lever for arm movement. Its shape and landmarks guide clinical assessment of shoulder function and injury.

sections.p: The scapula sits on the posterior thorax, forming the glenoid cavity for the humerus. It acts as a stable base for shoulder muscles and allows a wide range of arm motion.
b: Flat, triangular bone; glenoid cavity; key muscle attachments

sections.p: It lies on the posterior thoracic wall, articulating with the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint and with the humerus at the glenohumeral joint. The spine of the scapula runs from medial to lateral, ending in the acromion.
b: Acromion, spine, medial border, lateral border, glenoid cavity

sections.p: Anteriorly the scapula is covered by the deltoid and trapezius. Posteriorly it lies against the ribs and thoracic spine. The suprascapular notch and subacromial space are critical for rotator cuff function.
The scapular region receives arterial input from the suprascapular artery, dorsal scapular artery, and branches of the thoracodorsal artery.
b: Suprascapular artery; dorsal scapular artery; thoracodorsal artery

sections.p: Motor innervation comes from the suprascapular nerve, dorsal scapular nerve, and spinal accessory nerve. Sensory input is via the suprascapular and dorsal scapular nerves.
b: Suprascapular nerve; dorsal scapular nerve; spinal accessory nerve

sections.p: The scapula provides attachment for muscles that abduct, adduct, rotate, and stabilize the shoulder. Its mobility allows the arm to reach overhead and behind the back.

Common problems include winged scapula from long thoracic nerve injury, rotator cuff tears, and scapular fractures. Low-resource settings may see infections like osteomyelitis or TB affecting the scapula.
b: Winged scapula; rotator cuff tear; scapular fracture; osteomyelitis; TB

sections.p: Palpate the acromion, spine, and medial border to assess for winging. Ask the patient to shrug and abduct the arm; asymmetry suggests nerve injury.
b: Acromion palpation; shrug test; abduction test

whenToSeekHelp: Severe shoulder pain with inability to move arm; sudden loss of shoulder function; signs of infection such as fever and swelling

faq.a: Paralysis of the serratus anterior from long thoracic nerve injury, often due to trauma or surgical nerve damage.

faq.q: How is a scapular fracture diagnosed?
faq.a: Plain radiographs reveal cortical disruption; CT is used if complex fractures are suspected.

faq.q: Can the scapula be infected in low-resource settings?
faq.a: Yes, osteomyelitis or TB can involve the scapula; look for pain, swelling, and systemic signs.
